Sergeant Keshi Mabunda

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Meet the cop who is putting the country's top serial killers behind bars. Sergeant Kesha Mabunda goes beyond the line of duty and is reaping the rewards.

Unique Selling Point:
He had big dreams of becoming a lawyer but when he couldn’t afford law school, he switched things up and became a cop instead – and it’s a good thing he did.
Sergeant Keshi Benneth Mabunda is the man who brought Rosemary Ndlovu, believed to be South Africa’s worst female serial killer, to book.
Ndlovu, who was sentenced in 2021, is serving six life terms at the Johannesburg Prison for orchestrating the murders of her partner and five relatives to claim insurance payouts to the tune of R1,4 million.

When he was sworn in as a police officer, he made what many considered a bold promise, that he would fight crime in every barrough, and win. At the time it seemed like a distant dream; everyone knows that you can’t win the war against crime, especially coming from a small village in Giyani, Limpopo.

In an extraordinary short space of time, Khesi began to reap the rewards, being assigned to tough cases, graduating to detective status and making a mark wherever he worked. He has been hailed as the most charismatic and respected officer. It is his cutting-edge policing strategies and investigator tricks that has propelled him to a celebrity status. He was recently recognised by his peers and named national detective and forensic service employee of the year.

But for this cop, fame isn’t important – knowing Ndlovu is behind bars is all the reward he needs.
For three years he pursued the former policewoman and felt vindicated when the late Judge Ramarumo Monama not only convicted her but praised him for his watertight case.
Had it not been for Keshi, “the files would have been in the police station gathering dust”.



Summary:
Background:
>Growing up and his ambitions to study law but ending up in the police force
>What does he do for fun? What does he enjoy outside of work, safety considered? e.g. music, soccer, family get-togethers, etc.
>Public distrust in police force is widely reported and officers often make the headlines for behaving badly, criminally – to what extent does this motivate him to excel in his work?
Financial crimes/insurance cases:
>What kind of cases did he work when he started out as a detective, and how did he end up as a specialist of sorts in insurance crimes?
>Insurance cases often involve family members doing vile things to their relatives, and someone who deals mainly with these cases would be forgiven for harbouring feelings of mistrust when it comes to their own relatives. How does he separate his work from his family life and relationships?
>The nature of the crimes is often gruesome and heinous, to what extent does he make use of counselling and psychological support services?
>Does he exclusively work cases linked to insurance and financial crimes? Why is he so passionate about this type of crime specifically?
>How do insurers receive him in the execution of his work? Are insurance companies cooperative and happy to assist when they get a call from him about suspicious activity during his investigations?
>Having worked so many of these cases, what does he think is the one thing the insurance industry can do to curb these crimes?
Safety:
>In general police officers always have their lives on the line by virtue of their jobs but in his case, his success in putting criminals behind bars has made him a prime target. It's only natural that he would be fearful at times. How does he overcome these fears on an almost daily basis?
>How has his life changed now that safety is a priority for him? And has his family been drawn into his chaotic world e.g.he can't just go to a shopping mall with his family like other people do at month-end. He probably limits his use of social media where people share images and content of happy times with their family.
>Why does he soldier on despite his life being on the line? As we speak Rosemary stands accused of putting out a hit on him.

Rosemary Ndlovu:
>He was very emotional on the day Rosemary Ndlovu was found guilty. Why did this case matter so much to him?
>Did he feel a sense of betrayal in Rosemary? After all she was his colleague and a police officer, but she brought the uniform into disrepute and was running her shenanigans at the police station where they all worked together i.e. making copies of falsified documents in the office right next to his, using the printer and copier they all shared, loan sharks came looking for her at the police station they all worked at together. Did he feel personally offended by her behaviour?
Reputation as super cop:
>National detective and forensic service employee of the year – does he find that his peers in force trust his experience and expertise, and reach out for advice and guidance when dealing with their own cases? How is he imparting his skill and experience with his colleagues?
>How has his success at work changed the way people perceive him outside of work? His friends, people he grew up with?
Future plans:

Further information:
>Having achieved impressive success as a detective, does he see himself venturing into other aspects of policing, perhaps a senior role or a position in training others within the force?
Visuals wishlist:
Interview location:
>When interviewing him, ask him for a nice, cosy yet formal room at the police station. Don't interview him in his office as he's been interviewed there before. Only use his office for cutaways.
>Supporting interview suggestions - We will interview the station commander or captain about the value and pride in having an officer as dedicated as Mabunda as part of the team. Also, just to humanise him, can he suggest a friend of his that can be interviewed to talk about how much time they used to spend together before Mabunda's rise in the police and how things have now changed in terms of their friendship – still strong though they cannot do the things they used to do freely – only if this will not put his friend in harm's way.

Press Release:


Behind the Badge
In a quiet office in Johannesburg, Captain Keshi Mabunda mulls over a docket. It’s a startling murder case: a woman who allegedly killed two of her relatives to collect multi-million-rand pay-outs from their life insurance policies. This investigation is eerily like another case that Mabunda solved, and SAPS top brass have requested his assistance. In 2021, Mabunda was instrumental in the investigation that led to the arrest and conviction of notorious serial murderer, Rosemary Ndlovu. But even for a seasoned police officer, this is a dangerous job, and the bodyguards who occasionally accompany him suggest that Mabunda’s life is on the line. Carte Blanche meets the man behind the badge.  
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Claire Mawisa

Script:


INTRO – A North West mother of two dies suddenly in August last year. Just 30-years-old, Bonolo Modiseemang is in good health... that is, until she eats a sandwich made by her aunt. Hours later, she takes her last breath.
BREATHER
VO – Sorrow gives way to suspicion when it’s discovered a three million rand insurance policy has been taken out on Bonolo's life. The beneficiary is Agnes Setshwantsho... the aunt who'd made the sandwich.
BREATHER
VO – The case is eerily similar to one involving a notorious serial killer who murdered her relatives for hefty insurance payouts, Rosemary Ndlovu.

Police rope in a detective with a knack for solving complex murder-for-cash investigations... Keshi Mabunda.
LINK - We often see negative headlines about rogue cops that fuel public distrust in law enforcement. but every once in a while an officer comes along and reignites our faith in our criminal justice system.
VO – Mabunda comes from humble beginnings in Limpopo and didn't have specific plans for his future.
DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA - SAPS
I started school in 1981. I was just playing and going to school. I didn't have this career guidance at that particular time. - 02:40.
VO – But he did have a relative who was a lawyer.
VO – Unable to afford law school, he pursued what he thought was the next best thing... a career as a police officer.
VO – Mabunda's reputation grew as a thorough investigator who pays attention to seemingly insignificant details.
DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA – SAPS
30:06 - ... The time I was working here at this police station, every serious case was done by me. Whatever the case. House robbery or whatever.
VO – In 2015, he started working on the sinister Rosemary Ndlovu case.
BREATHER
LINK - Perhaps the biggest challenge Mabunda faces is that he not only solves heinous crimes but he deals with criminals that do the unthinkable to their own family members.
BREATHER
VO – It's 7am and Detective Mabunda drives past a location that is a constant reminder of the importance of his work... just a few metres from the police station is a patch of grass where the body of Maurice Mabasa was found with around eighty stab wounds.
BREATHER
VO - Maurice - who’d fathered a daughter with Rosemary - became her third known victim.
DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA – SAPS
She tried a lot of means to kill Maurice, but he survived. - 27:17
so she stabbed him multiple times to make sure that he loses his life. - 27:31
Shockingly, Rosemary was a police officer. It made her crimes especially hard to unravel because she was familiar with investigation methods and knew how to cover her tracks.
BREATHER
VO – By the time Bushie Engelbrecht left the SAPS, he had over forty years experience in investigations and was responsible for training new detectives to deal with serious crimes.
As far as he is concerned, serial murders are the toughest cases to crack…
BUSHIE ENGELBRECHT – RETIRED POLICE OFFICER
14:30 – To address serial killings, I call it a science. You have to do a geographical crime pattern. You have to do a modus operandi, you will have to work very extensively using informers but most importantly is to speak to people that knew the deceased and with whom was she connected.
BREATHER
DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA – SAPS
22:50 - ... I remember in Rosemary’s case, I had two best witnesses on my case.
23:02 - You know, I suffered to obtain a statement from them.
??? - When I went for the first time, they said, ‘We can't give you a statement because we're not, we don't trust you, police, you're crooks.’ - 23:45
VO – Mabunda had to sharpen another skill that helps detectives earn the trust of informants... patience.
DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA – SAPS
It happened one day, I was supposed to take them to consultation in the High Court. I was so busy preparing in the morning. - 24:39 - I sent my colleague to go fetch them and come back with them at the police station so I can take them to Johannesburg. When he arrived there, they told him straight that, ‘We dont want you here. Call him and tell him to come fetch us himself We dont know you. And don’t come here anymore.’ - 24:55 {Chuckles at the end of the byte}
24:56 - Then he came back alone. Then I said, ‘Ok, it’s fine.’ so I drove and fetched them and they gave me an earfull along the road. ‘Why do you send people to us?’ {Laughs} They said a lot of things. - 25:11
DETECTIVE SERGEANT MOHALE - SAPS
03:35 - I think it was very hard, especially when you deal with somebody who's working at the same department that you're working in, you know. A police officer who has access to the docket, access to information. - 03:50.
VO - Not only was Rosemary a member of the SAPS herself, she was also based at the same police station as the investigators.
Mabunda got creative and used the rumor mill to spread incorrect information.
DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA - SAPS
09:08 - She found out that I'm investigating the case … but she learned that I gave the case to another person. - 09:21
VO – In 2018 - four years into the investigation, and six victims later - Mabunda and his team finally caught Rosemary red-handed, coordinating a hit on what would have been her seventh victim… her own sister.
This video recording sealed her fate.
UPSOUND – WOMEN WHO KILL – ROSEMARY NDLOVU
07:55:13 – You know, I don't have money. I'm doing this to get a bit of money. - 08:00:12
VO – By then, Rosemary had pocketted around one point four million rands in insurance payouts. She planned to get more and targeted other relatives, including her mother.
In 2021, she was convicted and sentenced to six life terms.
DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA - SAPS
I was very much disappointed to see a police person doing such a crime and getting away with that crime. So I said, ‘Yeah, I must make sure. I don't want to make a mistake. This person must go.’ - 26:29
CLAIRE - 26:30 - Do you think she's remorseful? - 26:32
26:33 - I don't think so. I don't think so at all. Those are just crocodile tears or whatever. But she's so cruel. Evil, Rosemary.
BUSHIE ENGELBRECHT – RETIRED POLICE OFFICER
19:15 – I'm very proud about him, very, very proud. I've got gooseflesh. You know for a policeman to investigate another policeman, you must be what I call a true blue policeman, because if you see one committing corruption and you keep quiet, you're actually corrupt yourself.
BREATHER
Just two years after that high profile conviction, Setshwantsho, dubbed Rosemary 2.0, allegedly murdered her niece in an insurance fraud scheme. And in February this year, another charge relating to the murder of her son whom she’s insured for six million rands was added to the docket. It’s alleged her scheme extends to around 40 relatives.
BREATHER
LINK - Being a detective puts a target on the backs of crimefighters and Mabunda knows this better than most. And yet, even when he has to constantly look over his shoulder, he remains resolute.
BREATHER
DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA – SAPS
I do receive calls from prison whereby inmates will say, I will post bail for those particular people. They'll say, ‘No, we're going to get you. We know where you stay. We know where you frequent.’ - 18:13
BUSHIE ENGELBRECHT – RETIRED POLICE OFFICER
33:00 - The moment you take the oath to become a policeman and you start working after your training, you start working as a policeman, your life is always in danger.
34:12 – ... You can't move anywhere, you can't go for a pub lunch, you can't do this and that. The curtains are always drawn. You have firearms with you.
VO – Rosemary's threats, from behind prison walls, These threats have led to heightened security and lifestyle changes for Mabunda.
DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA – SAPS
18:14 - But I cannot stop doing my work because of those threats. But I just have to be extra careful by not finding myself at the wrong places. - 18:27
BREATHER
VO – Engelbrecht believes the country needs more detectives like Mabunda if we’re to reduce the high crime rate..
BUSHIE ENGELBRECHT – RETIRED POLICE OFFICER
25:19 – ... I saw a detective not long ago who showed me 700 dockets. I nearly fainted because it's impossible to make a success of any of those 700.
25:38 – That is why they become disillusioned and leave the service,
To aid with training challenges, Engelbrecht suggests that experienced retired cops should be roped in to mentor young detectives.
BREATHER
VO – Mabunda was awarded Detective of the Year and at this year’s function he was promoted to Captain.
UPSOUND
Mabunda collecting his award.
DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA – SAPS – AT SAPS AWARDS
CLAIRE - ??? - You say that you don't do your work for recognition, but how do you feel that your colleagues want you to be recognized? - 00:54
00:55:26 - It's a great honour for me. I didn't expect this, more especially this year.
01:08 - But it's a great pleasure when the National Commissioner said I must come here for a special award. Not just an award, but a special award. - 01:13

BREATHER VO – By the time Bushie Engelbrecht left the SAPS, he had over forty years experience in investigations and was responsible for training new detectives to deal with serious crimes. As far as he is concerned, serial murders are the toughest cases to crack… BUSHIE ENGELBRECHT – RETIRED POLICE OFFICER 14:30 – To address serial killings, I call it a science. I was so busy preparing in the morning. - 24:39 - I sent my colleague to go fetch them and come back with them at the police station so I can take them to Johannesburg. And don’t come here anymore.’ - 24:55 {Chuckles at the end of the byte} 24:56 - Then he came back alone. A police officer who has access to the docket, access to information. - 03:50. VO - Not only was Rosemary a member of the SAPS herself, she was also based at the same police station as the investigators. Mabunda got creative and used the rumor mill to spread incorrect information. I'm doing this to get a bit of money. - 08:00:12 VO – By then, Rosemary had pocketted around one point four million rands in insurance payouts. DETECTIVE KESHI MABUNDA - SAPS I was very much disappointed to see a police person doing such a crime and getting away with that crime. So I said, ‘Yeah, I must make sure. Those are just crocodile tears or whatever. But she's so cruel. Evil, Rosemary. BUSHIE ENGELBRECHT – RETIRED POLICE OFFICER 19:15 – I'm very proud about him, very, very proud. I've got gooseflesh. You know for a policeman to investigate another policeman, you must be what I call a true blue policeman, because if you see one committing corruption and you keep quiet, you're actually corrupt yourself. And in February this year, another charge relating to the murder of her son whom she’s insured for six million rands was added to the docket. It’s alleged her scheme extends to around 40 relatives. And yet, even when he has to constantly look over his shoulder, he remains resolute. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Meet the cop who is putting the country's top serial killers behind bars. Sergeant Kesha Mabunda goes beyond the line of duty and is reaping the rewards.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: He had big dreams of becoming a lawyer but when he couldn’t afford law school, he switched things up and became a cop instead – and it’s a good thing he did. Sergeant Keshi Benneth Mabunda is the man who brought Rosemary Ndlovu, believed to be South Africa’s worst female serial killer, to book. Ndlovu, who was sentenced in 2021, is serving six life terms at the Johannesburg Prison for orchestrating the murders of her partner and five relatives to claim insurance payouts to the tune of R1,4 million. When he was sworn in as a police officer, he made what many considered a bold promise, that he would fight crime in every barrough, and win. At the time it seemed like a distant dream; everyone knows that you can’t win the war against crime, especially coming from a small village in Giyani, Limpopo. In an extraordinary short space of time, Khesi began to reap the rewards, being assigned to tough cases, graduating to detective status and making a mark wherever he worked. He has been hailed as the most charismatic and respected officer. It is his cutting-edge policing strategies and investigator tricks that has propelled him to a celebrity status. He was recently recognised by his peers and named national detective and forensic service employee of the year. But for this cop, fame isn’t important – knowing Ndlovu is behind bars is all the reward he needs. For three years he pursued the former policewoman and felt vindicated when the late Judge Ramarumo Monama not only convicted her but praised him for his watertight case. Had it not been for Keshi, “the files would have been in the police station gathering dust”.
metadata.Summary: Background: >Growing up and his ambitions to study law but ending up in the police force >What does he do for fun? What does he enjoy outside of work, safety considered? e.g. music, soccer, family get-togethers, etc. >Public distrust in police force is widely reported and officers often make the headlines for behaving badly, criminally – to what extent does this motivate him to excel in his work? Financial crimes/insurance cases: >What kind of cases did he work when he started out as a detective, and how did he end up as a specialist of sorts in insurance crimes? >Insurance cases often involve family members doing vile things to their relatives, and someone who deals mainly with these cases would be forgiven for harbouring feelings of mistrust when it comes to their own relatives. How does he separate his work from his family life and relationships? >The nature of the crimes is often gruesome and heinous, to what extent does he make use of counselling and psychological support services? >Does he exclusively work cases linked to insurance and financial crimes? Why is he so passionate about this type of crime specifically? >How do insurers receive him in the execution of his work? Are insurance companies cooperative and happy to assist when they get a call from him about suspicious activity during his investigations? >Having worked so many of these cases, what does he think is the one thing the insurance industry can do to curb these crimes? Safety: >In general police officers always have their lives on the line by virtue of their jobs but in his case, his success in putting criminals behind bars has made him a prime target. It's only natural that he would be fearful at times. How does he overcome these fears on an almost daily basis? >How has his life changed now that safety is a priority for him? And has his family been drawn into his chaotic world e.g.he can't just go to a shopping mall with his family like other people do at month-end. He probably limits his use of social media where people share images and content of happy times with their family. >Why does he soldier on despite his life being on the line? As we speak Rosemary stands accused of putting out a hit on him. Rosemary Ndlovu: >He was very emotional on the day Rosemary Ndlovu was found guilty. Why did this case matter so much to him? >Did he feel a sense of betrayal in Rosemary? After all she was his colleague and a police officer, but she brought the uniform into disrepute and was running her shenanigans at the police station where they all worked together i.e. making copies of falsified documents in the office right next to his, using the printer and copier they all shared, loan sharks came looking for her at the police station they all worked at together. Did he feel personally offended by her behaviour? Reputation as super cop: >National detective and forensic service employee of the year – does he find that his peers in force trust his experience and expertise, and reach out for advice and guidance when dealing with their own cases? How is he imparting his skill and experience with his colleagues? >How has his success at work changed the way people perceive him outside of work? His friends, people he grew up with? Future plans:
metadata.Further information: >Having achieved impressive success as a detective, does he see himself venturing into other aspects of policing, perhaps a senior role or a position in training others within the force? Visuals wishlist: Interview location: >When interviewing him, ask him for a nice, cosy yet formal room at the police station. Don't interview him in his office as he's been interviewed there before. Only use his office for cutaways. >Supporting interview suggestions - We will interview the station commander or captain about the value and pride in having an officer as dedicated as Mabunda as part of the team. Also, just to humanise him, can he suggest a friend of his that can be interviewed to talk about how much time they used to spend together before Mabunda's rise in the police and how things have now changed in terms of their friendship – still strong though they cannot do the things they used to do freely – only if this will not put his friend in harm's way.
